prompt:
Extract every policy commitment stated in the text below.

Rules:
- One commitment per line.
- Write each as a verb phrase: an action followed by its object. For example: "raise the income tax threshold" or "build 300000 new homes".
- State each commitment at the level of a distinct policy action, not its implementation details. Do not subdivide a single commitment into steps.
- Include every commitment. Do not select, rank, prioritise, or judge importance.
- Use the text's own terms for policy objects. Do not substitute synonyms.
- Do not number the lines. No bullets, headings, preamble, or commentary.
- If the text states no policy commitments, output the single word NONE.

<text>
New Labour’s 1997 manifesto promises national renewal built on the principles “what counts is what works,” governing for “the many not the few,” and rebuilding trust through specific, deliverable commitments. It rejects both old left statism and Conservative laissez-faire, aiming for pragmatic, modern solutions across public services, the economy, and constitutional reform.

Economy and tax: Deliver stability for growth with a tough low-inflation target (2.5%), reform of the Bank of England to depoliticise monetary policy, and strict fiscal rules (borrow only to invest; keep debt at prudent levels). Stick to existing spending limits for two years; conduct a spending review to shift money from waste to priorities. No increase in basic or top income tax rates; long-term goal of a 10p starting rate; cut VAT on fuel to 5%. Fund a welfare-to-work drive via a windfall levy on excess profits of privatised utilities.

Jobs, skills, business: A major welfare-to-work programme will get 250,000 under-25s into jobs or training and incentivise hiring of the long-term unemployed. Create Individual Learning Accounts and a University for Industry; expand lifelong learning. Support competitive markets with tougher competition law; reinvigorate public–private partnerships for infrastructure; back small firms (cut late payment, red tape, better export support); establish Regional Development Agencies. Introduce a sensibly set National Minimum Wage via an independent Low Pay Commission; keep key 1980s union reforms while promoting partnership and recognition where a majority vote for it.

Education (number one priority): Cut class sizes to 30 or under for 5–7s by ending assisted places; universal nursery for four-year-olds; modernise comprehensives with setting, literacy/numeracy targets and summer schools; “fresh start” for failing schools; empower parents; General Teaching Council and better teacher training; wire schools to the internet and create a National Grid for Learning. Reform higher education finance with fair, income-related repayments.

NHS and public health: End the internal market; primary care-led planning with multi‑year agreements; cut admin to fund care (first £100m savings to treat 100,000 extra patients); end waits for cancer surgery; annual real-terms funding rises; new quality measures, more representative boards, eliminate mixed-sex wards. Ban tobacco advertising; create an independent Food Standards Agency.

Crime: “Tough on crime, tough on the causes.” Halve time from arrest to sentence for persistent young offenders; final warning system and Youth Offender Teams; more police on the beat; decentralise and strengthen the CPS; consistent sentencing with guidelines; tackle disorder and petty crime; new offences for racial harassment; pilot compulsory drug testing/treatment for offenders; free vote to ban all handguns.

Families, housing, pensions: A national childcare strategy; basic Child Benefit protected; support work–life balance (48-hour limit, holidays, unpaid parental leave with flexibility). Protect homeowners (action on gazumping; flexible mortgages) and revive social housing by releasing council house receipts; license HMOs; introduce commonhold. Keep the basic state pension (uprated at least with prices), retain SERPS as an option, create stakeholder pensions, and review long-term care funding via a Royal Commission.

Environment, transport, culture: Make every department a “green” department; integrated transport policy; strengthen rail regulation and create a rail authority; public–private partnership for London Underground; strategic roads review; promote low-emission vehicles and renewables; no case for new nuclear. Protect rural services, widen access to the countryside, free vote on hunting; create NESTA to back young talent; reform lottery distribution; back the 2006 World Cup bid.

Clean politics and the constitution: End hereditary peers’ voting rights; transparent party funding and ban foreign donations; Freedom of Information Act; incorporate the European Convention on Human Rights; devolution to a Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly after referendums; London mayor and strategic authority; regional chambers with optional elected assemblies by referendum; referendum on Commons voting reform.

Europe, defence, foreign policy: Lead reform in the EU (complete single market, enlarge to the East, reform CAP/CFP, greater openness; retain veto on key areas; sign the Social Chapter). On the euro, any entry requires Cabinet, Parliament, and a referendum. Defence through NATO; retain Trident; strategic defence review; ban anti-personnel landmines; stricter arms export controls. Create a Cabinet-level international development department, renew focus on poverty reduction and the UN 0.7% aid target; lead on climate change (aim to cut CO2 by 20% by 2010).

Five election pledges:
- Cut class sizes to 30 or under for 5–7 year-olds by using assisted places savings.
- Fast-track punishment for persistent young offenders by halving time from arrest to sentencing.
- Cut NHS waiting lists by treating 100,000 extra patients, funded by £100m saved from red tape.
- Get 250,000 under‑25s off benefit and into work with a windfall levy on utilities.
- No rise in income tax rates; cut VAT on heating to 5%; keep inflation and interest rates as low as possible.
